taboo.title: 避諱 naming taboos usable for dating, Song to Qing
taboo.method: Each fact cites at least two independent sources where found; entries with one source carry single_source: true. 陳垣《史諱舉例》卷八 is the primary reference; its 卷一/卷七 citations count as the same source.
caveats: Taboo evidence gives an earliest date (terminus post quem), not an exact date.
Chen Yuan's 史諱舉例 (1928) is the standard authority and the root of nearly every later account, so most rows rest on it alone; independent corroboration is rare, and where a row has it, it is cited.
Facsimiles, 影宋/影刻 reprints, lithographs and photo-reprints copy the taboos of their model and cannot be dated by them (韓春平; 善本古籍).
Practice was uneven even within one book; check several characters and other evidence (paper, layout, colophon).
Several substitutes (歷, 甯, 寕, 元) are also ordinary characters.

entries.fact: Song taboo practice was the strictest of any dynasty: up to ~50 characters per imperial name (homophones 嫌名 included), and taboos on earlier emperors (祧廟/舊諱) were still enforced (紹熙元年 1190 edict).
entries.collector_use: A Song-printed or Song-written text should show missing strokes (or substitutes) on the names of all earlier Song emperors and ancestors, not just the reigning one. The latest emperor whose name is avoided gives the earliest possible date; the first later emperor whose name is NOT avoided suggests the text predates him. A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.

entries.fact: Missing-stroke avoidance (缺筆, usually the last stroke) began in the Tang (first datable Tang stele example 乾封元年 666); before that only substitution or leaving a blank was used.
entries.collector_use: A 缺筆 form cannot be a pre-Tang avoidance; in Song and Qing material it is the most common form. A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.

entries.fact: The Yuan did not in practice avoid emperors' names (names were Mongol transcriptions); 海 for Wuzong 海山 was freely used. Formal rules from 延祐 (1314-1320) covered only memorial formats and the full name.
entries.collector_use: Do not expect taboo evidence in Yuan texts. A Yuan reprint (修補) of a Song block often shows Song taboos dropped on recut pages. A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.

entries.fact: For most of the Ming, imperial names were not avoided: the rule 二名不偏諱 (a two-character name is not tabooed when only one character is used) meant almost nothing was avoided, since nearly every Ming emperor had a two-character name. Avoidance became real only from the Wanli period onward and especially Tianqi-Chongzhen (an edict of 崇禎三年 1630 ordered avoidance of the temple names of 太祖, 成祖 and seven later emperors).
entries.collector_use: Taboo forms are useful only for late-Ming material (c.1620-1644): 常→嘗, 洛→雒, 校→較, 由 with a missing last stroke. Absence of avoidance says little about a Ming date before 1620. A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.

entries.fact: Qing avoidance began with the Kangxi emperor's Chinese name 玄燁 (Shunzhi's 福臨 and earlier Manchu names were not avoided); it was strictest under Yongzheng and Qianlong (literary inquisition, e.g. 王錫侯《字貫》case 1777) and loosened after Daoguang. From the Xianfeng emperor (1851) onward the first character of the emperor's name (shared with his brothers/generation) was not avoided; only the second was, by a missing stroke.
entries.collector_use: In a Qing text, each tabooed character shows the earliest reign the text can belong to; a text that avoids 玄 but writes 胤/禛 in full is probably Kangxi (1662-1722). A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.

entries.fact: Qing taboos on earlier emperors' names stayed in force to the end of the dynasty (1911/12) and were dropped by the Republic.
entries.collector_use: A text with 玄 missing its last stroke can be anywhere from Kangxi to 1911; only the LATEST avoided name narrows the date. After 1912 avoidance was no longer required, though reprints and conservative writers kept old forms. A taboo gives the earliest possible date, never a date.
